The p-value of a [t-test](basic-statistical-methods.qmd#def-two-sample-t-test)
comes from a distributional approximation:
the statistic is only approximately t-distributed unless the data are Gaussian.
A **permutation test** takes its null distribution from the data instead [@wikipedia_resampling_statistics].
If the null hypothesis says that two groups have the same distribution,
then under that hypothesis the group labels carry no information,
so reassigning the labels at random produces data sets that are as plausible as the observed one.
The spread of the test statistic across those relabelings is its null distribution.

This page defines exchangeability, the permutation distribution and the permutation p-value,
shows why that p-value is valid,
and then approximates it by random relabelings, which is how it is computed in practice.
It continues the [bootstrap](bootstrap.qmd) page's idea of computing a [sampling distribution](estimation.qmd#def-sampling-distribution) by resampling,
and supplies the p-values that the [multiple testing](multiple-testing.qmd) page corrects.
These notes follow chapter 13 of @james2021islr2e
and the treatment in @good2005permutation.
